stages.title: Answer mark
stages.text: The distant modem holds its high mark at 2,225 Hz. This excerpt starts at the first sound, after the telephone exchange has answered.

stages.title: Caller returns mark
stages.text: The caller adds a steady 1,270 Hz. Two pitches travel together, one in each direction. Both ends now have a carrier to detect.

stages.title: The terminal speaks
stages.text: The answering terminal sends “CARRIER ARCHIVE ONLINE” and a login prompt. Every zero pulls the high pitch down to 2,025 Hz. The caller still holds a steady mark.

stages.title: Reply from home
stages.text: The user sends “HELLO FROM HOME”. The lower voice now switches between 1,070 and 1,270 Hz. After the message both ends hold mark, ready for another character.

300.method: Reconstruction of a Bell 103A2 channel establishment, starting with the answer mark. The caller is already in data mode. The nominal 150 ms carrier-detection interval and additional 1.5 s wait come from Bell’s interface sequence. Payloads and typing delays are illustrative. Both messages are encoded at 300 bit/s, with one start bit, eight data bits and one stop bit. This is an ideal electrical signal with no acoustic-cup or line distortion.

sources.label: Bell System Practices 591-014-100, Table A · tone assignments
Bell System 103A interface specification, §6.2 · channel establishment

stages.title: Answer mark
stages.text: The answering modem sends repeated pairs of ones, each turning the carrier back by a quarter turn. This produces the steady high whistle that the caller recognizes.

stages.title: Caller trains
stages.text: The low band fills with scrambled ones. Although the underlying bit is always one, the scrambler supplies changing bit pairs so the receiver can find the symbol clock.

stages.title: Answer trains
stages.text: The high band changes from a whistle to a rough texture as the answering modem also sends scrambled ones. Both voices now make four possible phase steps.

stages.title: Login prompt
stages.text: The high band now carries an actual framed message, “CARRIER ARCHIVE ONLINE” followed by “LOGIN: ”. User data sounds much like scrambled training. The wire has no special connected chime.

stages.title: Reply from home
stages.text: The caller sends “HELLO FROM HOME”. Both transmitters continue sending scrambled idle ones after the characters run out.

1200.method: Transmitter reconstruction of the V.22 constant-carrier startup, beginning at the answer mark. The international V.25 preamble is omitted, as permitted on some national connections. The model follows nominal timing, differential quadrant changes, the 14/17-bit-tap scrambler and 75% roll-off pulse shaping at 600 baud. The guard tone is disabled. It assumes a clean line, no propagation delay and successful detection. Real equalizers, carrier offsets, speaker response and national compromise filters are outside the model. The 8N1 terminal messages and typing pauses are illustrative.

sources.label: CCITT V.22 (1988), §§2, 5 and 6.3 · modulation and startup

stages.title: Answer mark
stages.text: The answering modem sends repeated pairs of ones, each turning the carrier back by a quarter turn. This produces the steady high whistle that the caller recognizes.

stages.title: Request 2,400
stages.text: The caller alternates two particular pairs of bits, 00 and 11, for a tenth of a second. This short signature says it can use the larger alphabet.

stages.title: Answer accepts
stages.text: The answer modem returns the same signature in its own band. The caller has already switched to scrambled ones at 1,200 bit/s.

stages.title: Train at 1,200
stages.text: Both ends send scrambled ones. Each listens to the partner’s known pattern and prepares to distinguish points closer together.

stages.title: Sixteen signal points
stages.text: The answer modem switches to four bits per symbol. The caller follows about one tenth of a second later. The clock still ticks 600 times a second.

stages.title: Login prompt
stages.text: The high band now carries an actual framed message, “CARRIER ARCHIVE ONLINE” followed by “LOGIN: ”. User data sounds much like scrambled training. The wire has no special connected chime.

stages.title: Reply from home
stages.text: The caller sends “HELLO FROM HOME”. Both transmitters continue sending scrambled idle ones after the characters run out.

2400.method: Transmitter reconstruction of the V.22bis constant-carrier startup, beginning at the answer mark. The international V.25 preamble is omitted, as permitted on some national connections. The model follows nominal timing, differential quadrant changes, the 14/17-bit-tap scrambler and 75% roll-off pulse shaping at 600 baud. The guard tone is disabled. It assumes a clean line, no propagation delay and successful detection. Real equalizers, carrier offsets, speaker response and national compromise filters are outside the model. The 8N1 terminal messages and typing pauses are illustrative.

stages.title: Answer tone
stages.text: The answering modem sends 2,100 Hz with half-turn phase reversals, a request to disable network echo cancellation.

stages.title: Caller on the line
stages.text: The caller adds a steady 1,800 Hz. Its tone will overlap the answering modem’s signals.

stages.title: Time the round trip
stages.text: The answerer sends 600 and 3,000 Hz together. The ends take turns reversing phase, timing the replies to estimate delay.

stages.title: Train the receiver
stages.text: A regular S pattern and its brief reversal set the timing. The signal then opens into a reproducible stream of scrambled ones for echo and equalizer training.

stages.title: Advertise the rates
stages.text: The answering modem repeats a 16-bit R1 word offering 4,800 and 9,600 bit/s and trellis coding.

stages.title: Return the training
stages.text: The caller supplies its own known sequence. Each direction uses a different scrambler so the two signals can be distinguished.

stages.title: Choose the common mode
stages.text: The caller offers the simpler 16-point mode. The answerer trains again, selects 9,600, and both ends mark agreement with an E word.

stages.title: Enter data mode
stages.text: The caller switches to four information bits per symbol and sends scrambled ones. The answerer follows. The receivers open their data outputs after the final preamble.

stages.title: Connected · 9,600 bit/s
stages.text: The answerer now encodes the text “Welcome to the signal archive!” The caller sends “LIST”. Both messages repeat. The equal-looking fuzz now carries recoverable bytes in both directions.

9600.method: Synthesis begins at V.25 answer tone, after dialing and the initial off-hook silence. The caller answers after 1.02 s. V.25 permits early termination after detecting its response for 100 ms, so the 1.2 s tone is a permitted example. One-way delay is 10 ms. Training lengths and finite root-raised-cosine transmit filters are example choices. No channel or receiver is simulated. Includes reciprocal training, R1/R2/R3, E, scrambled B1 and synchronous 16-QAM data. The chosen payload repeats plain ASCII bytes least-significant bit first, with no link-layer framing.

stages.title: Answer tone
stages.text: The answering modem sends 2,100 Hz with half-turn phase reversals, a request to disable network echo cancellation.

stages.title: Caller on the line
stages.text: The caller adds a steady 1,800 Hz. Its tone will overlap the answering modem’s signals.

stages.title: Time the round trip
stages.text: The answerer sends 600 and 3,000 Hz together. The ends take turns reversing phase, timing the replies to estimate delay.

stages.title: Train the receiver
stages.text: A regular S pattern and its brief reversal set the timing. The signal then opens into a reproducible stream of scrambled ones for echo and equalizer training.

stages.title: Advertise the rates
stages.text: The answering modem repeats a 16-bit rate word offering all five V.32bis speeds, including 14,400.

stages.title: Return the training
stages.text: The caller supplies its own known sequence. Each direction uses a different scrambler so the two signals can be distinguished.

stages.title: Settle on 14,400
stages.text: While the caller repeats its rate offer, the answerer trains again and selects 14,400. Both transmit an end word. The short data-mode preamble that follows is outside this excerpt.

14400.method: Synthesis begins at V.25 answer tone, after dialing and the initial off-hook silence. The caller answers after 1.02 s. V.25 permits early termination after detecting its response for 100 ms, so the 1.2 s tone is a permitted example. One-way delay is 10 ms. Training lengths and finite root-raised-cosine transmit filters are example choices. No channel or receiver is simulated. Ends at the E words, before trellis-coded B1 and user data.

stages.title: A pulsing answer
stages.text: At 2,100 Hz the answer tone swells and shrinks 15 times a second. This V.8 variant also reverses phase at 450 ms intervals.

stages.title: Find a common language
stages.text: The caller sends its menu in the low V.21 band. The answerer repeats their common modes in the high band. Three framed zero bytes close the exchange.

stages.title: Exchange capabilities
stages.text: Each end sends a checked INFO0 message with its clock and carrier options. These brief words ride on different carriers.

stages.title: Measure the downlink
stages.text: The answering modem plays a 21-note chord for 160 ms, then the same chord 6 dB quieter. The four empty frequencies help reveal distortion.

stages.title: Measure the return path
stages.text: The calling modem sends the same two-level probe. The two ends can now compare estimates for each direction.

stages.title: Choose the symbol clock
stages.text: The example reports a clean path. The receiver’s results lead to a 3,200-symbol/s clock and 1,920 Hz carrier in both directions.

stages.title: Align the receiver
stages.text: An alternating pair marks the start of training. Six turns through a known 48-symbol pattern give the receiver a reference. Scrambled ones follow it.

stages.title: Train the other direction
stages.text: The caller sends S, the periodic PP sequence and four-point training on the selected carrier. Both modems learn their own echo while the far receiver learns its equalizer.

stages.title: Fine-tune both ends
stages.text: The answering modem marks the move to final training. Both directions now train at once using separate scrambled sequences.

stages.title: Agree on a rate
stages.text: The MP messages specify a maximum of 28,800 in each direction. Their acknowledgments and end markers conclude this excerpt.

28800.method: Synthesized V.8 menus, V.34 INFO messages with CRC, phase-reversal ranging, L1/L2, S, PP, four-point TRN, J, MP acknowledgments and E. This fixed clean-line scenario selects symmetric rates, zero frequency offset and no vendor-specific training. Pulse shaping, levels, receiver timing and training lengths are illustrative. Stops before the trellis-coded B1 preamble and payload. No recording or added noise.

stages.title: A pulsing answer
stages.text: At 2,100 Hz the answer tone swells and shrinks 15 times a second. This V.8 variant also reverses phase at 450 ms intervals.

stages.title: Find a common language
stages.text: The caller sends its menu in the low V.21 band. The answerer repeats their common modes in the high band. Three framed zero bytes close the exchange.

stages.title: Exchange capabilities
stages.text: INFO0 identifies the optional fast clock and the larger signal alphabet needed at 33,600. A dedicated bit advertises the larger constellation.

stages.title: Measure the downlink
stages.text: The answering modem plays a 21-note chord for 160 ms, then the same chord 6 dB quieter. The four empty frequencies help reveal distortion.

stages.title: Measure the return path
stages.text: The calling modem sends the same two-level probe. The two ends can now compare estimates for each direction.

stages.title: Choose the symbol clock
stages.text: The example reports a clean path. INFO1 selects about 3,429 symbols per second and a carrier near 1,959 Hz for both ends.

stages.title: Align the receiver
stages.text: An alternating pair marks the start of training. Six turns through a known 48-symbol pattern give the receiver a reference. Scrambled ones follow it.

stages.title: Train the other direction
stages.text: The caller sends S, the periodic PP sequence and four-point training on the selected carrier. Both modems learn their own echo while the far receiver learns its equalizer.

stages.title: Fine-tune both ends
stages.text: The answering modem marks the move to final training. Both directions now train at once using separate scrambled sequences.

stages.title: Agree on a rate
stages.text: Both MP messages enable 33,600 and request it in both directions. Their acknowledgments and end markers conclude this excerpt.

33600.method: Synthesized V.8 menus, V.34 INFO messages with CRC, phase-reversal ranging, L1/L2, S, PP, four-point TRN, J, MP acknowledgments and E. This fixed clean-line scenario selects symmetric rates, zero frequency offset and no vendor-specific training. Pulse shaping, levels, receiver timing and training lengths are illustrative. Stops before the trellis-coded B1 preamble and payload. No recording or added noise.

stages.title: Answer tone
stages.text: After a short silence the answering modem sends 2,100 Hz. Its strength ripples 15 times per second. Phase reversals ask network echo cancellers to stand aside.

stages.title: The menus agree
stages.text: Listen to the low caller and higher reply. At 300 bit/s they advertise data service, V.34 fallback and complementary V.90 roles. Three framed zero bytes acknowledge the agreement.

stages.title: Both ends probe
stages.text: Each end sends the same 21 pitches, first loud and then 6 dB quieter. The far end compares what it receives. This edit moves directly between the two probe bursts.

stages.title: Train the receiver
stages.text: A 48 ms repeating pattern briefly reverses, then opens into a steady hiss. A digital scrambler determines every sign in that hiss. The receiver knows what to expect and can correct the line’s smearing.

stages.title: Test the PCM levels
stages.text: Which levels survive the route? This example alternates a known reference with test levels of increasing magnitude. The recurring swells are the same 64-level scan repeated six times.

stages.title: Carrier acquired
stages.text: After final negotiation, 48 frames of known bits lead straight into a repeated text message, “CARRIER IS UP. HELLO FROM THE DIGITAL END.” Six samples now carry 42 bits. The remote speaker would usually be silent by this point.

56000.method: Edited synthesis at native speed. V.8 menus, line probes, Sd/TRN1d, a chosen digital-impairment pattern, and B1d into 56,000 bit/s payload use documented signal rules. The timeline cuts out INFO/ranging, most upstream training and the final parameter exchange. The last two sections use example parameters, including an ideal 64-level magnitude set and no spectral shaping. PCM is decoded with North American μ-law. Listen levels are scaled for playback. No line distortion, telephone speaker, or recording is modeled.
